name: Unit of Work
intent: Collect all the changes a business action makes, then write them together in one transaction, or not at all.
scenario: A checkout marks an order as paid, lowers the stock and adds loyalty points. If the third write fails, the first two must not stay.
problem: The checkout writes each change to the store as it happens. When a later write fails, the earlier ones are already saved: the order is paid, the stock is lower and the points are missing. Cleaning that up by hand is easy to forget and hard to test.
solution: A UnitOfWork object remembers the changes the action makes but does not write them. When the action finishes, commit() opens one transaction, applies every change and saves. If any write fails, it restores the earlier state and reports the failure. Callers only say what changed, and the unit decides when and how it is saved.
pain: Each change is written the moment it is made
A failure on the third write leaves two writes behind
Every write opens its own transaction
Rollback code is scattered through the checkout
benefits: Changes are saved together or not at all
One transaction per business action, not one per write
Failure handling lives in commit(), once
The action can be tested by looking at what it registered
whenToUse: One business action changes several records that must stay consistent
You use repositories or a data mapper and want one place that decides when to save
You want to batch writes and open fewer transactions
whenNotToUse: An action that changes one record: a single write is already atomic
Changes that span several databases or services: one unit cannot make them atomic
Your ORM session already tracks and flushes changes: use it rather than wrapping it again
pitfalls: A unit that lives for a whole session keeps stale data and holds locks for too long
Forgetting to call commit() makes the changes vanish without an error
The unit makes one database atomic, not a call to a payment provider: use a saga or an outbox for that
Reading your own uncommitted changes can surprise callers if the unit does not track them

roles.label: Client
roles.description: The business action, such as checkout. It registers changes and asks for a commit.

roles.label: Unit of work
roles.description: Remembers every new, changed or removed object, and writes them in one transaction on commit.

roles.label: Data store
roles.description: Where the changes end up. It can restore the earlier state if a write fails.

quiz.question: A checkout writes the order, then the stock, then the points, each straight to the database. The points write fails. What is the best way to stop paid orders with no points?
options: Retry the points write until it succeeds, since the first two writes have already worked
Register the three changes in a unit of work and save them in one transaction on commit
Write the points first, because that is the write that is the most likely to fail
Catch the error, log it and let the support team fix the order by hand later on
quiz.explanation: The need is all three writes or none. A unit of work collects the changes and applies them in one transaction, so a failure leaves nothing behind. Retrying may never succeed, reordering only moves the problem, and manual repair leaves broken data in the meantime.

quiz.question: A developer builds a unit of work that also calls the card provider inside commit(), after saving the order rows. The provider call fails after the rows are committed. What was the mistake?
options: The unit of work should have saved the rows after the provider call so that it could roll back
The card provider should have been wrapped in a repository so that it could join the unit
A unit of work makes one database atomic, and a remote call needs a saga or an outbox
The unit of work should have used a longer timeout so the provider call would not fail
quiz.explanation: A transaction cannot roll back a call to another system. Putting the call inside commit() only hides the gap. A saga with a compensating refund, or an outbox, handles the cross-system part. Reordering and timeouts do not make the two systems atomic.

quiz.question: A web app creates one unit of work when the server starts and reuses it for every request. Users see each other's half-finished changes and some saves fail with lock timeouts. What is the fix?
options: Create a new unit of work for each business action and discard it after commit
Add a global lock around commit() so that requests take turns to save
Make the unit of work a singleton with thread-safe collections inside it
Raise the lock timeout in the database so the saves have time to finish
quiz.explanation: A unit of work belongs to one business action. Sharing it mixes unrelated changes and holds locks far too long. A global lock, thread-safe collections and a longer timeout all keep the shared unit and hide the symptoms.
